Plasma-sprayed TBC systems typically consist of a low-pressure plasma-sprayed (LPPS) NiCrAlY or CoCrAlY bond coating and an air-plasma-sprayed yttria-stabilized zirconia insulative layer.
The LPPS process results in better bond strength and oxidation resistance compared to conventional air plasma spray.
Plasma-sprayed TBC systems incorporate 10-15% porosity and use partially stabilized zirconia compositions to achieve strain accommodation.
EB-PVD TBC systems deposit the ceramic layer with a columnar microstructure that provides excellent strain tolerance.
EB-PVD yttria-stabilized zirconia coatings have been tested to over 29,000 thermal cycles without failure.
Denser zirconia coatings, such as laser-glazed EB-PVD zirconia, exhibit lower erosion rates compared to medium porosity plasma-sprayed zirconia.
Toughness values in the range of 0.5 to 3.2 MPa√m have been measured for plasma-sprayed and EB-PVD yttria-stabilized zirconia coatings.
TBC systems can fail due to either tensile or compressive strains, leading to spalling of the ceramic layer.
The Garrett program aims to develop engine-mission-analysis-capable TBC life prediction models for both plasma-sprayed and EB-PVD TBC systems.
The program includes experimental quantification of failure modes and obtaining statistically significant design data to calibrate the TBC life models.
The program is divided into two phases: Phase I focuses on failure mode analyses and preliminary model development, while Phase II will develop a comprehensive, design-capable life model.
The program includes piggyback factory engine tests to validate the accuracy of the TBC life prediction models.
Nondestructive evaluation methods, such as eddy current technology, are being investigated to quantify TBC properties.
The program is using TBC systems produced by commercial suppliers Chromalloy, Klock, and Temescal.
Thermal cycling is necessary to fully develop the subcritical microcracking in plasma-sprayed yttria-partially stabilized zirconia coatings.
